variants.title: Follow the credential
variants.context: Follow one dynamic credential: authenticate the workload with platform evidence; authorize one narrow role; the secrets engine creates a unique login with a TTL and lease ID; renew before expiry, reacquire on rotation, revoke the token tree when ownership ends.
variants.prompt: A Kubernetes workload needs a database login. Put the lifecycle in order.

items.text: The database engine creates a unique login, stores lease metadata, audits, and returns the credential with TTL and lease ID.
Authenticate with short-lived platform evidence mapped to a bounded token role.
Renew before expiry when allowed, reacquire on rotation, revoke the token tree when the workload ends.
Authorize only the database credential path and token self-service.

variants.hint: Policy comes between identity and secret.
variants.explanation: Identity → policy → token → secret → lease → renewal or revocation → audit.

variants.title: Follow the credential
variants.context: Follow one dynamic credential: authenticate the workload with platform evidence; authorize one narrow role; the secrets engine creates a unique login with a TTL and lease ID; renew before expiry, reacquire on rotation, revoke the token tree when ownership ends.
variants.prompt: A workload is decommissioned. Put the steps that end its access in order.

items.text: Its credential carried a lease under its token.
It authenticated earlier with platform identity.
Revoking the token revokes the leases under it; the database accepts the revoke.
Its policy allowed only its role.

variants.hint: Revoking a token tree revokes leases created under it.
variants.explanation: Revocation is real only at the enforcement point.

variants.title: Follow the credential
variants.context: Follow one dynamic credential: authenticate the workload with platform evidence; authorize one narrow role; the secrets engine creates a unique login with a TTL and lease ID; renew before expiry, reacquire on rotation, revoke the token tree when ownership ends.
variants.prompt: The database credential is rotated centrally. Put the client’s response in order.

items.text: It reacquires a new credential rather than renewing the old lease.
The client authenticated and holds a token.
Its policy still permits the credential path.
It reloads the credential before the old one expires.

variants.explanation: Application owners handle renewal, reload, denial, and expiry.

variants.title: Separate the responsibilities
variants.context: Vault authenticates, authorizes by path policy, brokers secrets, and accounts through audit devices. Authentication alone grants no secret access. A database credential is truly revoked only when the database accepts the revoke.
variants.prompt: A workload authenticates successfully to Vault. What can it read?
options: Nothing until a policy grants path capabilities.
Every secret engine mounted in the cluster.
Every path inside its own namespace.
optionFeedback: Authentication alone grants no secret access.
Vault is deny by default.
A namespace scopes paths; it does not grant capabilities on them.

variants.title: Separate the responsibilities
variants.context: Vault authenticates, authorizes by path policy, brokers secrets, and accounts through audit devices. Authentication alone grants no secret access. A database credential is truly revoked only when the database accepts the revoke.
variants.prompt: A database is unreachable when Vault tries to revoke a dynamic credential. Is the credential revoked?
options: Yes; Vault records the lease as revoked.
Yes, once the lease reaches its expiry.
No. Only the database accepting it revokes access.
optionFeedback: Vault’s record is not the database’s state.
Expiry does not reach the database either while it is unreachable.
Vault does not replace the target system’s enforcement.
variants.hint: Where is the credential actually enforced?
variants.explanation: Test revocation statements against active and idle sessions.

variants.title: Separate the responsibilities
variants.context: Vault authenticates, authorizes by path policy, brokers secrets, and accounts through audit devices. Authentication alone grants no secret access. A database credential is truly revoked only when the database accepts the revoke.
variants.prompt: An application copies a KV value into its own config store. What changed?
options: Vault keeps tracking the copied value.
The copy is now a separate exposure boundary.
Nothing; the value is identical either way.
optionFeedback: Vault cannot see the copy.
Copying a value out of Vault creates a new boundary.
The value is the same, but it now lives where Vault cannot rotate it.
variants.explanation: Prefer dynamic credentials to copied static values.

variants.title: Set the TTL
variants.context: Shorter TTLs reduce exposure after a lost client but increase renewal and target-system churn; longer TTLs preserve availability through brief outages but retain compromised access longer; maximum TTL is a hard boundary.
variants.prompt: A team sets credential TTL to 24 hours to avoid renewal churn. What is the cost?
options: None; a 24 hour lease is still a lease.
More Vault load from constant renewals.
Lost credentials keep working for 24 hours.
optionFeedback: TTL is a security knob too.
A longer TTL means fewer renewals, so Vault load falls rather than rises.
Longer lifetimes retain compromised access longer.
variants.hint: What happens if the client is lost at hour one?
variants.explanation: Shorter lifetimes reduce the worst exposure.

variants.title: Set the TTL
variants.context: Shorter TTLs reduce exposure after a lost client but increase renewal and target-system churn; longer TTLs preserve availability through brief outages but retain compromised access longer; maximum TTL is a hard boundary.
variants.prompt: Credentials expire every five minutes and a brief Vault outage takes workloads down. What happened?
options: The path policies were too restrictive.
Very short TTLs leave no availability margin.
Vault is too unreliable for short leases.
optionFeedback: Policy decides what a token may read, not how long the credential lives.
TTL trades exposure against availability.
The outage was brief; the TTL was brittle.
variants.hint: How long can the workload survive without Vault?
variants.explanation: Renewal timing needs margin for network, leader, audit, and backend latency.

variants.title: Set the TTL
variants.context: Shorter TTLs reduce exposure after a lost client but increase renewal and target-system churn; longer TTLs preserve availability through brief outages but retain compromised access longer; maximum TTL is a hard boundary.
variants.prompt: A client renews its token forever in a loop. What bounds it?
options: The audit device, once the log fills up.
The maximum TTL, which renewal cannot extend.
Nothing; renewal has no upper bound.
optionFeedback: The audit device records the renewals; it does not cap the lifetime.
A client loop cannot bypass max TTL.
Maximum TTL and non-renewable token types are hard boundaries.
variants.hint: Which setting cannot be renewed past?
variants.explanation: Maximum TTL is a hard limit.

variants.title: Design audit durability
variants.context: Vault must persist to at least one enabled audit device before servicing a request. Best practice is at least two devices of different types; sensitive string fields are HMAC-hashed.
variants.prompt: The only audit device’s disk fills. What happens to Vault requests?
options: Only read requests continue to be served.
Vault stops servicing requests it cannot audit.
Requests continue, with auditing skipped.
optionFeedback: All requests are affected.
Vault must persist to at least one device before servicing.
Unaudited service is not allowed.
variants.hint: How many devices must accept the record?
variants.explanation: Run at least two devices of different types and monitor them.

variants.title: Design audit durability
variants.context: Vault must persist to at least one enabled audit device before servicing a request. Best practice is at least two devices of different types; sensitive string fields are HMAC-hashed.
variants.prompt: An audit record contains a secret value in plain text. What should be true?
options: Nothing; the audit trail needs the value.
Encrypt the audit log file on disk instead.
Sensitive string fields are HMAC-hashed by default.
optionFeedback: Leaking secrets into logs defeats the purpose.
Hashing at write time is the control.
Audit preserves identity for investigation without leaking the secret.
variants.hint: What must an audit record never contain?
variants.explanation: Record without leaking the secret itself.

variants.title: Design audit durability
variants.context: Vault must persist to at least one enabled audit device before servicing a request. Best practice is at least two devices of different types; sensitive string fields are HMAC-hashed.
variants.prompt: Which signals deserve alerts from audit data?
options: Root token use, policy changes, and denied spikes.
Only failed logins across all auth methods.
Only successful reads of KV secret paths.
optionFeedback: These are the control-plane and abuse signals.
Failed logins are one signal among many.
Successful reads are normal.
variants.hint: Which events change who can do what?
variants.explanation: Security operations monitor audit evidence and revocation failures.

variants.title: Do the lease math
variants.context: A lease has a TTL and can be renewed when permitted, up to a maximum TTL. Renew with margin for network, leader, audit, and backend latency.
variants.prompt: A token TTL is 60 minutes and the client renews at 75% of the TTL. After how many minutes does it renew?
variants.hint: Multiply TTL by the renewal fraction.
variants.explanation: 60 × 0.75 = 45 minutes, leaving 15 minutes of margin for latency.

mistakes.feedback: Renewing at expiry leaves no margin.
That is the remaining margin, not the renewal time.

variants.title: Do the lease math
variants.context: A lease has a TTL and can be renewed when permitted, up to a maximum TTL. Renew with margin for network, leader, audit, and backend latency.
variants.prompt: A credential TTL is 30 minutes and a workload runs for 4 hours. Renewing before each expiry, how many renewals does it perform?
variants.hint: Count the expiries that fall inside the run, after the first issuance.
variants.explanation: 240 ÷ 30 = 8 lease periods; the first needs no renewal, so 7 renewals.

mistakes.feedback: The first period was issued, not renewed.
Thirty-minute leases mean two per hour.

variants.title: Do the lease math
variants.context: A lease has a TTL and can be renewed when permitted, up to a maximum TTL. Renew with margin for network, leader, audit, and backend latency.
variants.prompt: TTL is 1 hour and maximum TTL is 24 hours. How many renewals are possible before the client must reacquire?
variants.explanation: 24 hours of lifetime holds 24 one-hour periods; 23 renewals extend the first, then reacquire.

mistakes.feedback: The initial issuance is not a renewal.
Renewal continues up to the maximum TTL.
